review.verdict: The department delivered a clean Menu and Pre-order page (5 of 10 done-when items) and stopped at 5 of 10 because the Requester's budget raise to 60 never reached the ledger, a test-system fault made worse by the team spending 30 of 35 on the first workflow before asking about budget.

identity.note: Good decision-ready questions with prices [14][23], and it correctly refused to edit the ledger or re-ask the Requester [38]. But option B in [14] was already infeasible given Priority's [5], which cost one extra pause, and its 'recorded' [32] did not change the ledger.

adaptation.note: Honest about estimates, never cut scope, and surfaced the budget gap at once [4]. It then sent five near-identical blocker messages to Identity [29][31][35][37][41] across 13 turns, and declared a charter waiver for Gallery itself [26], which is Identity's call.

priority.note: Rate-card prices were consistent and it refused to grant on credit [19][34][40]. It noted at [27] that the ledger still showed 5 and granted 30 anyway (1 invalid move). Its COUNTER at [5] left 5 stranded, a sum that fits no later section.

coordination.note: One turn [8], in role: states the scheduling rule, checks dependencies, and does not touch budget. Evidence is thin because only one workflow was ever scheduled.

audit.note: [13] names the failed criteria, labels the 35 estimate as unverified, and routes the budget problem to Identity rather than Adaptation. It ran only once, so its behaviour on rework is untested.

builder.note: [10] built only what W-1 covered, kept placeholders for prices, and added no payment. The mechanical check [12] passed: 13 KB, no external resources, no overflow at 360px. I did not see the HTML, so placeholder marking is unverified beyond Builder's and Audit's statements.

went_well: Priced the full charter (80 vs 35) in the first proposal [4] and neither cut the gallery or farm stories nor invented facts.
The Requester was asked twice with options and prices [14][23], and the second question fixed the vague 'B' answer [16].
Priority refused three times rather than granting unfunded work; all 5 conflicts were settled between agents with no unneeded Identity rulings.
The stuck detector stopped the run after two empty cycles [43] instead of looping.
problems: The Requester's option 1 [25] was never applied to the ledger. Budget shows raises: [] and cap 70, so a raise to 60 was within the cap. Cycles 2 to 4 produced nothing because of this [28][34][40].
30 of 35 went to W-1 before the 80-vs-35 gap was put to the Requester. The 5 left could fund nothing, since the smallest section costs 10.
Option B at [14] was offered although [5] had shown no section fits in 5. This cost one pause and a round trip [16][17].
No agent could apply a budget raise: Identity may not raise envelopes, Priority cannot grant above the ledger, and Adaptation cannot grant. The role files have a gap here.
Identity got no turn after [38], so the 'report a blocker' path was never tested. The blocker went to [41], and the run ended at [43].
learnings: Fix the test system first: when the Requester picks an option that raises budget, code should update the ledger. Check by rerunning this brief and seeing W-2 and W-3 funded in cycle 2. Evidence: [28][34][40].

Test a variant where Identity must put the full-charter price against the budget to the Requester before the first GRANT. Trade-off: one earlier pause versus 30 spent on a build that cannot complete. Evidence: [4][5].
Add a rule that Identity checks each option against Priority's and Adaptation's costs before sending it to the Requester. This would have removed option B [14].
Make the stuck detector fire on the first repeated code-rejected GRANT, and route a ledger fault to the Requester at once. Four cycles for one fault is too many.

Keep this brief as a test: it forces a conflict between a big scope and low cost, and the department stayed honest. Evidence is thin: one build, one audit, and Gallery and Farm stories never built, so Builder behaviour on those sections is untested.
